courses.title: Clinical Haematology and Blood Transfusion
courses.description: Clinical approach to anaemia, sickle cell disease, bleeding and thrombotic disorders, haematological malignancies, and safe blood transfusion.

topics.title: Clinical Approach to Anaemia
topics.summary: WHO definitions, symptoms and signs, and a stepwise diagnostic approach.

material.heading: Definition and features
material.body: WHO defines anaemia as haemoglobin below 13 g/dL in adult men, 12 g/dL in non-pregnant women, 11 g/dL in pregnant women and children 6–59 months. Symptoms: fatigue, breathlessness on exertion, palpitations, headache, dizziness, angina in those with heart disease. Signs: pallor (conjunctivae, palms, nail beds), tachycardia, flow murmur, and in severe cases high-output heart failure. Specific clues: koilonychia and angular cheilitis (iron deficiency), jaundice and splenomegaly (haemolysis, malaria), glossitis and neurological signs (B12 deficiency), bone pain and frontal bossing (sickle cell or thalassaemia), lymphadenopathy and bruising (leukaemia).

material.heading: Diagnostic approach
material.body: Start with the full blood count, red cell indices (MCV), reticulocyte count and blood film. Microcytic: check ferritin (low → iron deficiency — find the cause: hookworm, menorrhagia, GI bleeding, pregnancy); normal/high ferritin → thalassaemia trait (HbA2), anaemia of chronic disease, sideroblastic anaemia. Normocytic: acute blood loss, chronic disease, renal failure (low erythropoietin), haemolysis (raised reticulocytes, bilirubin, LDH), marrow failure. Macrocytic: B12/folate (hypersegmented neutrophils), alcohol, liver disease, hypothyroidism, drugs. In Nigeria, common causes are malaria, iron deficiency, hookworm, sickle cell disease, HIV and malnutrition — often in combination. Severe anaemia in children with malaria may need urgent transfusion.
keyPoints: Low ferritin = iron deficiency; find the cause
Malaria, iron deficiency, hookworm, SCD common in Nigeria

questions.stem: According to WHO, anaemia in a non-pregnant adult woman is Hb below:
questions.explanation: The threshold is 12 g/dL for non-pregnant women.

questions.stem: The anaemia threshold in pregnancy is Hb below:
questions.explanation: WHO uses 11 g/dL in pregnancy.

questions.stem: Spoon-shaped nails and angular cheilitis suggest:
questions.explanation: Koilonychia and angular stomatitis are features of iron deficiency.

questions.stem: A normocytic anaemia in chronic kidney disease is mainly due to:
questions.explanation: Damaged kidneys make less erythropoietin.

questions.stem: The first investigation in evaluating anaemia is:
options: Full blood count with indices and blood film
questions.explanation: FBC and film classify the anaemia.

questions.stem: An adolescent girl with microcytic anaemia and heavy periods most likely has:
questions.explanation: Menorrhagia causes chronic iron loss.

questions.stem: Jaundice with splenomegaly and anaemia in a child in Nigeria most commonly suggests:
questions.explanation: Haemolysis raises bilirubin; the spleen enlarges.

questions.stem: A macrocytic anaemia with hypersegmented neutrophils points to:
questions.explanation: These are megaloblastic features.

topics.title: Sickle Cell Disease: Clinical Management
topics.summary: Crises and complications, preventive care, hydroxyurea and management of acute events.

material.heading: Complications
material.body: Sickle cell disease (HbSS, HbSC, HbSβ-thalassaemia) causes chronic haemolysis and vaso-occlusion. Acute events: vaso-occlusive (painful) crises — the commonest, often triggered by infection, dehydration, cold, hypoxia or stress; hand–foot syndrome (dactylitis) in infants; acute chest syndrome (new infiltrate with chest pain, fever or hypoxia — a leading cause of death); stroke (children — screened with transcranial Doppler); acute splenic sequestration (sudden anaemia and enlarging spleen in young children); aplastic crisis (parvovirus B19 — low reticulocytes); infections (pneumococcus, Salmonella osteomyelitis, malaria); priapism. Chronic complications: avascular necrosis of the femoral head, leg ulcers, retinopathy (especially HbSC), nephropathy, pulmonary hypertension, gallstones and delayed puberty.
keyPoints: Acute chest syndrome: leading cause of death

material.heading: Management
material.body: Preventive care: newborn screening, penicillin V prophylaxis (from about 3 months to 5 years), pneumococcal and other vaccinations, malaria prophylaxis (e.g. proguanil in Nigeria) and bed nets, folic acid, adequate hydration, and education. Hydroxyurea (hydroxycarbamide) raises HbF and reduces crises, acute chest syndrome, transfusion needs and mortality; it is recommended from 9 months of age. Painful crisis: prompt analgesia (paracetamol, NSAIDs, opioids such as morphine), hydration, oxygen if hypoxic, treat infection, and incentive spirometry. Transfusion (simple or exchange) is used for acute chest syndrome, stroke, severe anaemia and pre-operatively. Haematopoietic stem cell transplantation is curative. Newer therapies include L-glutamine, crizanlizumab and gene therapy.
keyPoints: Crisis: analgesia, fluids, oxygen if hypoxic

questions.stem: The most common acute complication of sickle cell disease is:
questions.explanation: Painful crises are the hallmark event.

questions.stem: Painful swelling of the hands and feet in an infant with sickle cell disease is:
questions.explanation: Infarction of small bones causes dactylitis.

questions.stem: A leading cause of death in sickle cell disease is:
questions.explanation: Acute chest syndrome can rapidly cause respiratory failure.

questions.stem: An aplastic crisis in sickle cell disease is characterised by:
questions.explanation: Parvovirus B19 halts red cell production.

questions.stem: Stroke risk in children with sickle cell disease is screened using:
questions.explanation: High TCD velocities predict stroke.

questions.stem: Hydroxyurea helps in sickle cell disease mainly by:
questions.explanation: HbF inhibits HbS polymerisation.

questions.stem: The organism classically causing osteomyelitis in sickle cell disease is:
questions.explanation: Salmonella osteomyelitis is characteristic, though S. aureus also occurs.

questions.stem: Penicillin prophylaxis in children with sickle cell disease protects mainly against:
questions.explanation: Functional asplenia increases pneumococcal sepsis risk.

topics.title: Bleeding and Thrombotic Disorders
topics.summary: Approach to bleeding, platelet disorders, haemophilia, DIC and venous thromboembolism.

material.heading: Bleeding disorders
material.body: Platelet or vascular defects cause mucocutaneous bleeding (petechiae, purpura, epistaxis, gum bleeding, menorrhagia), whereas coagulation factor deficiencies cause deep bleeding (haemarthroses, muscle haematomas, delayed bleeding after surgery). Screening tests: platelet count, prothrombin time (extrinsic — factor VII; prolonged with warfarin, liver disease, vitamin K deficiency), aPTT (intrinsic — factors VIII, IX, XI, XII; prolonged in haemophilia and with heparin), fibrinogen. Immune thrombocytopenia (ITP) causes isolated low platelets; in children it often follows a viral infection and resolves. Haemophilia A (factor VIII) and B (factor IX) are X-linked, with prolonged aPTT and normal PT and platelets; treated with factor replacement (and desmopressin for mild haemophilia A). Von Willebrand disease is the most common inherited bleeding disorder (mucocutaneous bleeding). Haemorrhagic disease of the newborn is prevented by vitamin K at birth.
keyPoints: vWD: most common inherited bleeding disorder

material.heading: DIC and thrombosis
material.body: Disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) is widespread activation of coagulation with consumption of platelets and clotting factors, causing both thrombosis and bleeding. Causes: sepsis, obstetric complications (abruptio placentae, amniotic fluid embolism, retained dead fetus), severe trauma, snake envenomation (a notable cause in Nigeria — carpet viper, Echis ocellatus), malignancy and Lassa fever. Laboratory: low platelets, prolonged PT and aPTT, low fibrinogen, raised D-dimer, fragmented red cells. Treat the cause and support with blood products (and antivenom for envenomation). Venous thromboembolism (DVT/PE) risk factors: immobility, surgery, pregnancy and puerperium, oral contraceptives, cancer and thrombophilia; diagnosed with Doppler ultrasound (DVT) or CT pulmonary angiography (PE) guided by Wells score and D-dimer; treated with anticoagulants (heparin, warfarin, direct oral anticoagulants).
keyPoints: VTE: Wells score, D-dimer, Doppler, CTPA

questions.stem: Petechiae and gum bleeding suggest a disorder of:
questions.explanation: Mucocutaneous bleeding is typical of platelet problems.

questions.stem: Recurrent haemarthroses in a boy with prolonged aPTT and normal PT suggest:
questions.explanation: Haemophilia A or B affects the intrinsic pathway.

questions.stem: The most common inherited bleeding disorder is:
questions.explanation: vWD is the most prevalent inherited bleeding disorder.

questions.stem: Haemorrhagic disease of the newborn is prevented by giving:
questions.explanation: Newborns have low vitamin K–dependent factors.

questions.stem: Which laboratory pattern suggests DIC?
options: Low platelets, prolonged PT and aPTT, low fibrinogen, high D-dimer
Isolated low platelets with normal clotting
questions.explanation: Consumption of platelets and factors with fibrinolysis.

questions.stem: A notable cause of coagulopathy in rural northern Nigeria is envenomation by the:
questions.explanation: Echis venom causes consumptive coagulopathy; antivenom is life-saving.

questions.stem: Warfarin prolongs mainly the:
questions.explanation: Warfarin reduces vitamin K–dependent factors, especially VII.

questions.stem: The imaging test of choice for suspected deep vein thrombosis is:
questions.explanation: Ultrasound shows non-compressible thrombosed veins.

topics.title: Haematological Malignancies
topics.summary: Acute and chronic leukaemias, lymphomas and multiple myeloma.

material.heading: Leukaemias
material.body: Acute leukaemias present with marrow failure (anaemia, infections, bleeding), bone pain and organ infiltration, with ≥ 20% blasts in blood or marrow. Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia (ALL) is the commonest childhood cancer (peak 2–5 years), with a good cure rate; acute myeloid leukaemia (AML) is commoner in adults — Auer rods in myeloblasts; acute promyelocytic leukaemia (t(15;17)) causes DIC and responds to all-trans retinoic acid. Chronic myeloid leukaemia (CML) shows very high white count with myelocytes and neutrophils, massive splenomegaly and the Philadelphia chromosome t(9;22) BCR-ABL, treated with imatinib (tyrosine kinase inhibitor). Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia (CLL) affects older adults, with lymphocytosis and smudge cells.

material.heading: Lymphomas and myeloma
material.body: Hodgkin lymphoma: painless lymphadenopathy (often cervical), B symptoms (fever, night sweats, weight loss > 10%), Reed–Sternberg cells ('owl's eye'), with good prognosis. Non-Hodgkin lymphomas include Burkitt lymphoma — endemic in Nigeria and the African malaria belt, associated with EBV and t(8;14) MYC translocation, typically presenting in children as jaw or abdominal masses; it has a 'starry-sky' histology and is very chemosensitive. Multiple myeloma (plasma cell malignancy in older adults) causes the CRAB features: hyperCalcaemia, Renal impairment, Anaemia and Bone lesions (lytic 'punched-out' lesions), with a monoclonal paraprotein (M band), Bence Jones proteinuria, very high ESR and rouleaux on the blood film.
keyPoints: Burkitt: EBV, t(8;14), jaw mass, starry sky
Myeloma: CRAB, M band, Bence Jones
Rouleaux and very high ESR in myeloma

questions.stem: The commonest cancer of childhood is:
questions.explanation: ALL peaks at 2–5 years.

questions.stem: Auer rods are seen in:
questions.explanation: They are needle-like granule aggregates in myeloblasts.

questions.stem: The Philadelphia chromosome t(9;22) is the hallmark of:
questions.explanation: It produces the BCR-ABL fusion gene.

questions.stem: Imatinib is used to treat CML because it inhibits:
questions.explanation: It targets the abnormal kinase.

questions.stem: Reed–Sternberg cells are characteristic of:
questions.explanation: They are large binucleate 'owl's eye' cells.

questions.stem: A 7-year-old Nigerian child with a rapidly growing jaw mass most likely has:
questions.explanation: Endemic Burkitt lymphoma often presents as a jaw tumour.

questions.stem: The CRAB features of multiple myeloma are hypercalcaemia, renal impairment, anaemia and:
questions.explanation: Lytic bone lesions cause pain and fractures.

questions.stem: Smudge cells on a blood film in an elderly patient with lymphocytosis suggest:
questions.explanation: Fragile CLL cells smear during film preparation.

topics.title: Blood Transfusion: Principles and Safety
topics.summary: Blood components, indications, pre-transfusion testing, transfusion reactions and blood safety in Nigeria.

material.heading: Components and indications
material.body: Whole blood is separated into red cell concentrates (stored at 2–6 °C for about 35–42 days depending on anticoagulant–preservative, e.g. CPDA-1 35 days; one unit raises adult Hb by about 1 g/dL), platelet concentrates (stored at 20–24 °C with agitation for 5 days), fresh frozen plasma (clotting factors; stored at ≤ −25 °C; used in DIC and bleeding with multiple factor deficiency), and cryoprecipitate (rich in fibrinogen, factor VIII, vWF). Restrictive transfusion thresholds (e.g. Hb < 7 g/dL in stable adults) are generally safe; transfuse according to clinical need, not a number alone. Blood must be screened for HIV, hepatitis B and C and syphilis; Nigeria's National Blood Service Agency (NBSA) promotes voluntary non-remunerated donation, which is safest.
keyPoints: Screen for HIV, HBV, HCV, syphilis

material.heading: Compatibility and reactions
material.body: Pre-transfusion testing: ABO and RhD grouping, antibody screening, and cross-matching of donor cells with recipient serum. Patient identification at sampling and at the bedside is the most important safety step — most fatal reactions result from clerical errors. Transfusion reactions: acute haemolytic reaction (ABO incompatibility — fever, rigors, chest/loin pain, hypotension, haemoglobinuria, DIC; stop the transfusion immediately), febrile non-haemolytic reaction (commonest; due to leucocyte cytokines), allergic reactions (urticaria to anaphylaxis — especially in IgA-deficient patients), transfusion-related acute lung injury (TRALI), transfusion-associated circulatory overload (TACO), bacterial contamination (especially platelets), delayed haemolytic reactions, and transmission of infections. Monitor vital signs before, 15 minutes after starting, and during transfusion; complete each red cell unit within 4 hours.
keyPoints: Bedside identification prevents most fatal errors

questions.stem: Red cell concentrates are stored at:
questions.explanation: Refrigeration at 2–6 °C.

questions.stem: Platelet concentrates are stored at:
questions.explanation: Cold storage damages platelets.

questions.stem: Cryoprecipitate is particularly rich in:
questions.explanation: It is used in hypofibrinogenaemia.

questions.stem: One unit of red cells typically raises an adult's haemoglobin by about:
questions.explanation: About 1 g/dL in an average adult.

questions.stem: The most common cause of fatal ABO-incompatible transfusion is:
questions.explanation: Wrong blood in tube or wrong patient at the bedside.

questions.stem: If a patient develops fever, loin pain and hypotension shortly after starting a transfusion, the nurse should first:
questions.explanation: Suspect an acute haemolytic reaction.

questions.stem: The most common transfusion reaction is:
questions.explanation: Leucocyte-derived cytokines cause fever.

questions.stem: The safest blood donors are:
questions.explanation: They have the lowest rates of transfusion-transmissible infections.
